content_metadata.description: An educational video discussing the role of crystal growth and defects in photographic chemistry, focusing on twinning in silver halide crystals and its significance in photographic processes.

qAndA.answer: The ions on the twin plane are arranged in a mirror image pattern, creating a discontinuity in the crystal lattice.
qAndA.question: In the diagram illustrating twin planes, what is the pattern of ions on the twin plane?

qAndA.answer: Excess bromide (Br-) or an acidic environment can promote the formation of octahedral AgBr crystals.
qAndA.question: What are two conditions that can promote the formation of octahedral AgBr crystals?

qAndA.answer: Plates provide a large surface area for photons to interact with the silver halide crystals, leading to exposure. They also provide surface area for the deposition of sensitizers and developers.
qAndA.question: Why are plates important in photographic processes?

qAndA.answer: The 1,1,1 crystal face is highly sensitive to differences in silver and halide ion concentrations and tends to grow faster than other faces, leading to twinning.
qAndA.question: What is the significance of the 1,1,1 crystal face in twinning?

qAndA.answer: Defects, particularly edge defects created by twinning, provide sites for enhanced chemical activity, which is crucial for the photographic process.
qAndA.question: Why are defects considered beneficial in silver halide emulsions?

activities.description: Explaining twin crystal formation and its relation to the 111 face.

activities.description: Emphasizing the importance of plate structure for photographic processes.

narrativeProgression.description: Highlights the significance of plates, particularly for providing surface area for photon absorption, chemical interactions, and deposition of sensitizers and developers.

props.name: Title: "Crystal Faces," Text explaining the importance of crystal faces, the 200 and 1,1,1 faces, and their roles in crystal growth.

Two diagrams representing the 200 and 1,1,1 crystal faces with alternating positive and negative charges (blue and green for 200 face) and text describing each face's arrangement and growth conditions.

scenes.thematicElements: Crystal faces, 200 face, 1,1,1 face, surface area, photon absorption, chemical reactivity, sensitizers, developers.

activities.description: Discussing the role of twinning in creating defects and enhancing chemical activity.

narrativeProgression.description: Explains the essential role of twinning in creating defects that are crucial for the functioning of silver halide emulsions, emphasizing that these defects make the photographic process work.

props.name: Title: "Twins Create Defects," Text explaining the role of twin planes as defects and their significance in silver halide emulsions.

Diagram illustrating a twin plane within a hexagonal plate, with text explaining that a twin creates edges for enhanced chemical activity and highlighting the benefits of hexagonal plates in terms of surface area for light exposure and process chemistry.

scenes.thematicElements: Twin planes, defects, chemical activity, surface area, light exposure, process chemistry.
scenes.title: Role of Twinning and Defects

videoEditingDetails.description: Static slide with text and diagram.

activities.description: Further explaining twin crystals and edge defects.

narrativeProgression.description: Reiterates the concept of twinning as a mirror image and emphasizes the 'out of step' arrangement of ions, concluding by listing the benefits of edge defects for photographic processes.

props.name: Title: "Twin Crystals," Text explaining where ions get out of step in twin crystals.

Diagram illustrating a crystal lattice with a twin plane, labeled "crystal lattice" and "twin plane." Text explaining that twinning is common and that twins are mirror images where growth changes direction.

Title: "Edge Defects Created by Twins," Text listing the advantages of edges, including high surface area, imbalance of surface ions, areas for enhanced light absorption, and greater chemical reactivity.

timecoded_text_to_speech.text: Welcome to the series Photographic Chemistry, presented by the foundation of the American Institute for Conservation of Historic and Artistic Works.
This program was made possible by grants from the National Endowment for the Humanities and the Andrew W. Mellon Foundation.

Each program in this series is presented as a short video. Depending on your video viewer, you should be able to pause, return to a previous section, or skip ahead to a later section by using a scroll bar or on-screen icons.
You will find an outline of the course and short quizzes to test your understanding on the course webpage.
There can be very unique effects now when we take advantage of this known fact that one face grows faster than another in a cubic relationship.
We can get the various types of silver halides that we sometimes see in the more modern 20th century silver halide emulsions, the plates, and plates that seem to be growing on top of plates.
When there are a series of plates growing one on top of the other, this is known as twining.
Plates and twines occur when one face grows preferentially faster than all the others.
Again, we notice that the one on one face is the most sensitive to differences in silver or halide concentration because these are faces which are pure in one of the ions.
If I have an acid based emulsion, I'm going to get accelerated growth of the one on one face.
If I have a highly basic ammonia or anomalical emulsion, then I'm going to get very accelerated rate of growth along the one on one.
There's a real balance there. I can dial or tweak in between the two to get the different crystal shapes that I want.
Plates are very important because they provide a lot of surface area.
They provide surface area for photons which translates into exposure.
They provide surface by which we can deposit chemistry, sensitizers, developers, and some of the chemistry that we'll talk about a little bit later.
This formation of twin plates is the introduction of what is most critical about silver halide grains, the reason why they work.
In solid state chemistry, the reason why silver halide works is because they're defective. They actually have defects.
A twine creates a defect. It creates sites or edges which enhance chemical activity where enhanced chemical activity will occur.

At the bottom of this slide, if you see I'm moving ions in the direction of the one on one face, and they're all the same ions, either you can imagine these being all halides or all silver, a twine is where they get out of step.
They start growing in one direction and then they sort of slip and the plate starts growing into the other direction.
You end up with this twine plate. A set of plates with an edge as shown on the right hand side of the slide.
It's a mirror image. It starts out one plate shape and then it starts taking off in another direction. It's almost like you've taken two plates and you glued them together.
This is known as a twine and it creates what is known as an edge defect. And on these edges, you've got high surface area, you've got imbalance of surface ions.
And this is going to be the site where a lot of very interesting photochemistry happens.
You have completed this unit. Depending on your video viewer, you should be able to scroll back to any point in the video as desired.
The short quiz found in the course materials on the website may help you confirm your understanding of the concepts introduced here.
Many thanks to the instructor, production editor, coordinator, and the collaborative workshops in photograph conservation committee for their work to make this program possible.
